content: A 21-year-old male with a history of sickle cell anemia experienced recurrent episodes of acute rheumatic fever starting at the age of 14. By the age of 16, he had developed mitral valve insufficiency and stenosis. While on prophylactic antibiotics, he remained free of recurrent episodes until three weeks prior to his final hospital admission, when he developed an upper respiratory infection. Subsequently, he experienced acute migratory polyarthritis, which was accompanied by a rapid decline in cardiac function, ultimately leading to his death. At autopsy, the heart was found to be enlarged, weighing 675 grams, with significant enlargement of the left atrium. Both the aortic and mitral valves exhibited fibrosis and fresh, small verrucae, which are characteristic of acute rheumatic fever. A gross photograph of the mitral valve revealed marked thickening and fibrosis of the valve leaflet. Numerous foci of fibrinoid necrosis were observed within the cusps, along with friable vegetations (verrucae) along the lines of closure. These irregular, wart-like projections were located at sites of erosion on the inflamed endocardial surface. The verrucae likely formed due to fibrin deposition at points where the valve leaflets come into contact. A low-power photomicrograph of heart tissue showed relatively normal-appearing tissue at this magnification. However, a higher-power photomicrograph of the myocardium revealed cellular accumulations known as Aschoff bodies within the interstitial tissue, particularly around blood vessels. Another high-power photomicrograph of the myocardium demonstrated the cellular details of an Aschoff body. These structures are composed of foci of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by lymphocytes, macrophages, occasional plasma cells, and plump, activated histiocytes referred to as Anitschkow cells or Aschoff cells. These distinctive cells have abundant amphophilic cytoplasm and central, round-to-oval nuclei with chromatin arranged in a slender, wavy ribbon resembling a caterpillar, hence the term caterpillar cells. In another high-power photomicrograph, an Aschoff body was observed containing what appeared to be a multinucleated Aschoff giant cell.
